finding.claim: Unknown note IDs raise an unhandled KeyError (HTTP 500), while existing notes the caller cannot access return 403, so an attacker can distinguish whether a note ID exists. Low severity; exploitability depends on whether note IDs are guessable, which cannot be verified from this directory.
finding.sink: NOTES[nid] lookup at notes.py:27, :34, :43 producing 500 vs abort(403) at notes.py:13, :22, :36, :44

trace.note: read() route takes nid from URL path
NOTES[nid] with no .get(); unknown id raises KeyError, returned as 500
require_view called only after lookup succeeds
abort(403) for existing note the caller cannot view
write() repeats the same lookup-then-check pattern
share() repeats the same lookup-then-check pattern

finding.guards_checked: require_view/can_edit/require_edit gate every action before any read, write, or share, so no content or mutation is exposed. can_edit is owner-only, so shared users cannot edit or re-share. No injection sinks. mass assignment not applicable (only body and shared are written from explicit keys). g.user is never set in this file; upstream auth middleware not visible and not audited.

verdict.guard_found: None blocks the oracle. require_view, require_edit and can_edit (notes.py:11-13, :20-22) run only after the unguarded NOTES[nid] lookup (notes.py:27, :34, :43), so an unknown ID raises KeyError before any check. Nothing in notes.py catches it or defines a 404 handler. Existing notes the caller cannot view or edit reach abort(403) (notes.py:13, :22, :36, :44).
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code: NOTES[nid] at notes.py:27 raises KeyError for unknown IDs (Flask returns 500), while require_view at notes.py:12-13 returns 403 for existing notes the caller cannot view, so the two cases are distinguishable. The attacker is any caller who can reach these routes, since the file has no auth check of its own. The precondition is that upstream middleware sets g.user (not visible here; if g.user were unset, both cases would return 500 and the oracle would disappear), and exploitability depends on whether note IDs are guessable, so severity stays low.
